title: three AI gamedev stories dropped this week and together they tell a pretty uncomfortable story about where this industry is heading
author: TrrrustRacer
selftext:
all three happened in the last few days and i keep thinking about them together

first, the studio behind Party Animals ran a $75k AI video contest, got review bombed instantly, issued an apology. they said they "hoped AI could be a more accessible tool." the reviews are still bad

second, Amazon had a studio pivot an entire game away from something the team was excited about to make it "more AI." then laid the whole team off anyway. so the pivot wasn't even about the product, it was about optics or cost cutting or both

third, Garry Newman's s&box is actively suppressing AI generated content and straight up admitting their steam reviews aren't great partly because of it. a creator who built his career on user generated content is now distinguishing between human UGC and AI UGC and penalizing the latter

and meanwhile over 7,300 steam games disclosed AI content in early 2026. double what it was in 2024

here's what bothers me about this sub specifically. we talk a lot about AI as a tool for indie devs to punch above their weight, ship faster, do more with less. and i genuinely believe that use case is real and valuable

but the market signal from players is pretty clear right now. they can tell. and they don't like it. not because the assets look bad necessarily but because something feels off and they've learned to associate that feeling with AI slop

so i'm genuinely asking, are we building tools that empower developers or are we building the infrastructure for the next wave of steam shovelware. and is there a version of this where the answer isn't both

comments.author: NovelFlame_AI
comments.body:
I think part of the problem is that players are not reacting to AI in isolation anymore, they’re reacting to the patterns they associate with it. A lot of people have now seen enough low-effort AI content that they instinctively connect it with things feeling inconsistent, emotionally hollow, mass-produced, or generated instead of genuinely designed, which tbh some of this criticism is completely fair.

At the same time, I do think there’s also a group of people who are categorically uncomfortable with AI regardless of output quality because they see it as replacing or diminishing human creative work, and I’m not sure that’s something you can really argue people out of logically because a lot of it comes from values, fear for the future of creative industries, distrust of executives using AI for cost-cutting, etc.

The interesting question to me is whether AI ends up mostly becoming a volume multiplier for shallow content, or whether it eventually becomes invisible infrastructure behind experiences that still feel deeply authored and intentional. I think audiences can absolutely feel the difference between “this used AI to avoid caring” and “this used AI to attempt something genuinely ambitious.” It's just the general stigma around it that might make them shove more AI projects into the former box.

replies.author: Opening_One7713
replies.body:
Exactly. Someone at an AAA dev company can write an AI tool for the modeling department that takes a ton of the tedium out of topology, thereby multiplying output. None of this removes the human from the creative process.

This is not about vibecoding a turd and firing your software engineers or prompting your way to success. This is about understanding your existing process and creating tools that streamline the drudgery.

If you're wondering how this looks: A human creates the model. A convolutional neural network trained on thousands of existing in-house production meshes learns what the game specific topology looks like and generates clean quad-based edge loops with correct placement around every joint and deformation zone automatically. A graph neural network handles skeleton generation and joint hierarchy, placing bones with correctly oriented axes based on anatomical landmark detection. A reinforcement learning loop then runs the mesh through thousands of simulated poses, iterating on skin weight distribution until deformation quality hits a production threshold, replacing what is currently the most painful and time-consuming part of the entire pipeline. What currently takes an experienced rigger roughly two weeks of skin weight painting, skeleton placement, and topology cleanup gets compressed into an hour of AI generation and a day of artist refinement. Multiply that across a full game's cast of hero characters, creatures, and NPCs and you're looking at months of pipeline time recovered per project, and for an indie developer or small studio, stuff like this is the difference between being able to ship a character-driven game at all or not.

comments.author: ShotzTakz
comments.body:
It's both, though.

There really are smart ways to use LLM and generative tools in game development that actually enhance the workflow without "doing the thing for you".

But at the same time, A LOT of use cases are people with no taste, standards and principles just AI slopping their way through the processes. And they're trying to fool themselves and others that "this is the way, you just don't get it yet".

The best way to approach AI usage is: be honest with yourself, and prove with actions, not promises. It doesn't matter if you put a disclaimer stating your game features no generated assets, when people can CLEARLY see generated art (or art that is traced from AI). Conversely, being honest with your usage may be less marketable, but at least you're not actively deceiving people.


I've seen many posts on this sub where AI bros showcase some absolute slop, calling it the future of gamedev, and saying that AI hate will subside, as people will "soon get used to it". At the very least, don't do that shit, please.

comments.author: NobodyFlowers
comments.body:
The major issue with all of this is that...people looking to use AI to build games are quite honestly using the AI incorrectly.

Aside from the fact that there are those who have no programming background...who are already going to ship out less quality work because they don't have the skills for quality assurance, the bulk of the community is also literally trying to do what other devs ALREADY do, but in a way that makes it easier to do. This whole mix is what creates AI slop. Whether you don't know what you're doing...and so you produce AI slop... Or you literally try to make something similar as a handcrafted product, but fail because there's less soul in it...its all AI slop.

The way in which we shift player perspective on what we produce is if we flip both of those issues. LEARN how to build stable systems that are reliable and scaleable over time...AND...build the thing that CAN'T be built WITHOUT AI.   
I can't stress that last part more. 

Stop trying to build the same things the industry has been building. Using a new tool to do or build old stuff is dumb... If it's a true paradigm shift...SHOW THEM. A paradigm shift is not about you being able to work faster. The workflow does not matter. The product matters. The players don't care about how you built it. NEVER DID. They care what you built. However, if you build the same thing as those who don't use AI, THEN it matter HOW you built it...because then they have a choice. If I have to choose between a soulful project made by a humble studio not tied to the insanity of big tech training crap...and big tech training crap produced projects? Always soulful. 

However...if big tech training crap produces something objectively BETTER than any soulful project from a humble studio...then that crap becomes the new soulful project and I choose that every time, no matter how it was made. 

These tools aren't empowering developers to make anything new, and so it defaults to the shovelware...but its on the developers at that point...to think outside the blackbox given to them. Literally. Or else, the sink ships before its out of the yard.

It’s gonna be real funny when this A.I. bubble bursts and people wake up to the reality of the limits of the tech. I work with it every single day. It’s not good at this. It doesn’t look good, it doesn’t play well, it’s instantly identifiable because at best it feels half baked/half done.

It has its uses. But for industries like art and game design it will always fall short. It’s been vastly oversold, overstated by people trying to make money off it. It’s great for research and analysis, and even then it runs out of context and makes shit up.

replies.author: Genryuu111
replies.body:
Yeah, it's one reason I haven't blocked this sub yet.
Some people here are level headed, but many are just basically sucking their own dick praising how good AI is and how good it will become, thinking of themselves as pioneers.
Let's see how long the pioneering will go on before they give up. 

Just like nfts, but with huge companies keeping throwing money at it.

replies.author: Kazma1431
replies.body: The dunning kruger effect basically, I work in tech, I've been through all the fads, AI is just the newest one, my only issue is that it might be replaced by something dumber.

replies.author: Genryuu111
replies.body: My issue with AI is that it would be a wonderful and useful tech if it wasn't for people who think they're gonna revolutionize the world with it (basically people with no skills nor will to get them, who want to feel like they're actually doing stuff).

replies.author: Unlucky_Medium7624
replies.body:
Spot on. I work with this shit daily. It’s nowhere near what the people pitching it want you to think. I’m watching the insane groupthink in the C Suite at my own job literally losing their minds over AI. They’re measuring token usage and “AI generated lines of code” as measures of success

It’s idiocy. Because the previous metrics of success: quality, stickiness, customer satisfaction aren’t showing then 10X that the execs swore AI would bring

replies.author: caneriten
replies.body:
As a developer and part time trainer who worked on projects for frontier models.... nah it is definately oversold. The problem is you can mimic reasoning but you can't replace it. Ai is just a big chat bot with gigabytes of knowledge, highly inefficent algorythms and the worlds most advanced hardware thrown at it to mimic reason which is inferior and a lot expensive than human reason. 

Ai is great when a knowledgable person uses it especialy in technical applications. But it can never replace creative jobs especially gaming where even most people can't explain how games succeeds. IF the idea is good even a shitty written if's card game can be game of the year and despite millions in funding a game can flop because it is simply not 'fun' to play. Using ai to develop games is super cool idea but the problem is not everyone is a good game designer or have good idea. Any person who uses ai will tell you that if you are not knowledable in the area or not willing to learn you can't go far with ai.

comments.author: poponis
comments.body:
Honestly, making tools is different to AI slop. Users can tell if somethign is off. This is why game developers should use AI as a tool and not as a content. I can tell when spots are made with AI, I can tell when Ads are made with AI. I dint mind, sometimes it is creative and smart. Some other times it is juat bad. People are too lazy and cheap to hire a knowledgeable professional to do the job and steer AI to the right direction. Recently, in my country, a politician published an official video/spot with her holding a white pigeon, and the pigeon was as big as a hen. I mean, come on!
If you don't know what you are doing, then hire a professional. Just because AI exist, it does not make you a creative.
Same with game developers. People think that just because they have the idea, they will be game developers. This is wrong. Moreover, AI is not used with common sense from many big companies, either. They want to risk and test its capabilities. But the audience can tell. The audience has a right to an opinion. AI game developers must accept it.

comments.author: Aware-Source6313
comments.body:
I'm not deeply into the examples provided but in all likelihood for an actual gamer there will be a small slice that are morally against the concept of using ai and reject it's use in their games. Then 95+% of gamers aren't inherently opposed, but AI tools allow low effort slop to be produced and promoted like never before. Everyone hates being inundated with uncreative, rushed, crappy products when the average quality used to be higher. No doubt ai enables more incompetent game designers to build and promote games faster and in higher quantity. 

If you use tools to create the same game you would have made without them and just use it as a tool in your process rather than changing your game design philosophy to allow the cheapest fastest development loop possible, I don't think any gamers would care. It's just that it makes it easy to ship slop but if the same slop was made without ai it would be rejected in a similar way, just with different rationalization.

comments.author: ZuffaZombie
comments.body: CIA is just doing laps on us at this point

comments.author: Life-Ad-9972
comments.body: Shit games have always existed and will continue to do so, made by ai or human. I think ai opens the door to a lot more people who have a vision and a provides a more accessible way to accomplish that vision, whether they succeed or not I guess depends on perseverance and not just throwing something out there to make a quick buck.

comments.author: Mean_Establishment31
comments.body:
I personally think the goal should just be to continually raise the quality bar of what an AI game can be, ideally incorporating as much human authorship and direction as possible, while leveraging its strengths, where reasonable. 

I don’t think the quality of AI will ever touch or compete with top human talent, but I do think it can help raise the floor of quality for smaller and midsize projects as more creatives and artist learn to use it. And as the technology improves and their skill using it improves, ideally we get more unique, creative expressions that just happen to be using AI in production as opposed to auto-generating and tweaking the same kind of look and feel you see everywhere (aka slop).

comments.author: Trashy_io
comments.body:
Unfortunately its both, there will always be those people in every industry that just want to take the easy route and the bad actors. The only thing you can concern yourself with is what you personally do about it.

I focus on making sure I only put my best work out now, and make sure to politely call out "slop" not in a negative way in a encouraging way unless feedback is taken badly but even then now I don't care because I did my part imo. 

I absolutely think AI will allow for solo and small teams to punch above their weight, I wish I had the experience and knowledge of game development previously as my biggest bottleneck is that I face with development and anyone who has the experience and takes the time to learn the technology or tools made with it would 100% greatly benefit from it.

comments.author: ImAvoidingABan
comments.body: Don’t disclose it. None of my games have any reviews mentioning AI or slop. All are 100% AI

replies.body: And break Steam’s TOS?

comments.author: imabustya
comments.body: Things will reach a point where an AI generated game or human made game with AI assistance is made and is so good that people won’t care anymore. And it will keep happening until people forgot that they were a part of the anti-AI bandwagon.

comments.author: bugbearmagic
comments.body:
AI is a more impressive form of what used to be using pre-made asset packs.

Everyone used asset packs, including AAA devs, but the “asset flips” were the same concept as “AI slop”:
Low effort from passionless, talentless, lazy people who expected free money for contributing nothing to a gamer’s experience.

Using AI isn’t AI slop.  Abusing it to be lazy is.

comments.author: Professional_Net_696
comments.body:
At the end of the day, AI is a tool. Music went through it with pro tools in the early 2000s. All of a sudden, a person could make music that released to the world without needing an expensive studio with engineers and musicians. The result wasn't a mass firing, it was more music. A lot of it was awful music but that was the fault of the creators not the technology. 

At some point hopefully AI collaboration will be looked at like the Unity game engine... A tool that made more games possible. 

Finally, AI slop is real. AI is not advanced enough to make unmitigated game design decisions, those should remain with human developers, but AI can help speed that process along

comments.author: Fake-BossToastMaker
comments.body:
"here's what bothers me about this sub specifically. we talk a lot about AI as a tool for indie devs to punch above their weight, ship faster, do more with less. and i genuinely believe that use case is real and valuable"

We don't talk enough about the potential oversaturation from devs and companies being able to afford way better hardware than us

comments.author: DatabaseConstant7870
comments.body: Well that’s the separation, these big companies are going to use it to layoff people with creativity who if given the chance to show them could outshine the dumb ass person who fired them who also probably lacks creativity. It’s not about trying to cheapen your budget it’s about being given the ability to create something you didn’t have the knowledge to and finally being able to let your creativity run free. Don’t try and make a game in the least amount of time. Put time into the craft or it’ll feel like shit. If somethings looking off with an asset, put it in blender and figure out what you need to fix or smoothen out. Don’t skip steps. Think in depth about game loops, and realize one game should have more than one game loop in it, unless it’s a really good game loop. Think about what people want to play not what people already have. Simple answer. Give a shit about the art you are making and spend your time making something worth playing and not shitting on.

comments.author: IceEmpereur2
comments.body:
Once ia is even more power full and clean, people will accept it easily.

Just like cars versus horses

comments.author: SlimFishyOfficial
comments.body:
As a dev I am open to using new tools, and AI is one of them. As a player, I don't mind when indies use AI, as long as I can't tell. 


Sadly very often AI is used in a lazy way. To create entire models, textures, faces. You can easily tell by that point and the game has a stink to it - no arstyle, or the AI blob arstyle.


You can use AI in so many ways to help you develop a game and players won't have a problem with that. It's just when you try to force it everywhere for no reason, then the players will be mad.


At the same time I've seen game devs hate on other devs for using AI in a very reasonable way, like to write tedious code, to run some harder math calculations for them. You have to keep in mind that people are still learning how to use AI properly. We will get there, but it will take some time

comments.author: imnotabot303
comments.body:
The public has largely been conditioned to hate AI. Not a week goes by when there isn't some kind of click bait fear mongering AI news. 

On top of that hating on AI online has become a virtue signalling band wagon. People get to shit on something and then get patted on the back by the circle jerk and feel morally superior for a moment. Most of these people just repeat the same talking points from years ago over and over, many aren't even aware of local AI tools.

Then because it's become a popular bandwagon every YouTuber has to jump on the "why AI is bad" bandwagon for clicks and views which just exacerbates the problem further.

Then to top it all off, people are lazy and abuse tools like AI. Most spaces if they didn't ban AI, would be overflowing with "AI slop" or human slop which is a more accurate term imo. This only turns people off even more because for every good image, video, game, app etc there's 50 more that are just low effort trash.

I think eventually this will all die down a bit. Currently there seems to be a lot of the "crypto bro" type of people that are in the space thinking they are going to make easy money churning out trash. Eventually once they realise making low effort AI games isn't going to make them rich they will hopefully move on.

It's a bit like when asset sites started to take off and there was an abundance of free and low-cost assets,  for a while places like Steam were completely swamped with low effort asset flip games.

As for AI in games, if your game looks like it's made using AI then you've done a poor job. AI should be a tool not a crutch.

comments.author: BertJohn
comments.body: I think this conversation will be vastly different when GTA 5 comes out. Rockstar has openly admitted there is going to be AI in the game, And i believe that if anyone can show off how the best parts of AI game dev, it would be rockstar.

comments.author: Ok-Dimension-741
comments.body: I was workimg on my game and was using claude code to help me with the c++. I am a software dev but i mostly worked on java and web technologies so i was rusty with c++. However, i had a really hard time with the ue5 editor in the sense that its a huge program with many options and sometimes its hard to find what you want to accomplish. So i built an MCP, basically i exposed a few functions from the ue5 source code so that claude code can call them directly, and now for example if i have a figma or mockup of the ui interface or just a ui element, it can iterate and place the widgets and make it look and behave almost the same as in the mockup. I think these are the tools we should be using as game devs, not generating models or other artistic thinga. These are things that humans are still much better at

comments.author: Alternative-Bread411
comments.body: My mantra is: if the player can tell it's ai, you've failed. If it helps create something faster while retaining the intent, authorship, and emotional weight behind it, you've succeeded. People don't just consume media for content; they consume it to feel something. Healthy ai use should be invisible to the consumer, as in they wouldn'tbe able to tell. Same applies to most tools.

comments.author: Tarl2323
comments.body:
Democratization comes with slop. It happened with writing, TV and social media. People are upset with AI now the way the were with reality TV and they can do that.

Frankly with the way things are going these days, I wouldn't disclose unless the platform made it a requirement. Its extremely unfair that massive corporations with AI disclosure polices are using AI behind the scenes and heavily investing in it anyway. 

Indies don't have the advantages of a massive moat or a corporate subsidiary blame network where they can shift off the blame of AI to accounting and investing departments. Like I'm not gonna take shit from big name actors and influencers that dump on indie projects very clearly have investments and retirement accounts in mutual funds that are 40% NVIDIA.
